analysis.one_liner: Caps seniors' yearly Medicare drug costs at $3,100 and makes drug makers give discounts at the pharmacy.
analysis.headline: Introduced by one Republican with one Democratic cosponsor, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was filed and never received a committee action or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would remake Medicare's prescription drug benefit starting in 2024: it would eliminate the 'donut hole' coverage gap, cap enrollees' yearly out-of-pocket drug costs at $3,100, cut the standard coinsurance from 25% to 20%, and let enrollees facing big drug bills spread their costs in capped monthly installments instead of paying large amounts at the pharmacy counter. To help pay for it, brand-name drug makers would have to provide a discount at the point of sale once a beneficiary passes the yearly deductible, with civil fines for companies that don't comply. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The tens of millions of people enrolled in Medicare Part D, especially those with expensive prescriptions: they would face no coverage gap, a $3,100 annual out-of-pocket cap, a lower 20% coinsurance, and the option to pay their share in capped monthly installments rather than large lump sums.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare enrollees with high drug costs

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates the Medicare Part D coverage gap beginning in 2024 by setting the coverage-gap cost-sharing formula to $0 for 2024 and later years.
Caps enrollees' annual out-of-pocket drug costs at $3,100 for 2024, with the cap adjusted upward each year thereafter.
Cuts the standard beneficiary coinsurance in the initial coverage phase from 25% to 20% starting in 2024.

Requires brand-name drug manufacturers to provide discounted prices at the pharmacy or mail-order point of sale once a beneficiary passes the annual deductible, backed by civil money penalties equal to the unpaid discount plus 25% for companies that fail to comply.

Automatically enrolls high-cost enrollees in an option to have their out-of-pocket costs capped and billed in monthly installments, with an opt-out, so a serious illness doesn't produce one large pharmacy bill.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, through mandatory point-of-sale discounts (10% off the negotiated price for drugs dispensed after the deductible), and Part D insurers, through sharply reduced federal reinsurance payments, new administrative duties, and unsettled monthly-payment balances treated as plan losses.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and Part D insurers

drawbacks.text: The bill does not lower drug prices themselves: it shifts who pays existing prices by requiring a 10% manufacturer discount after the deductible, but includes no government price negotiation or list-price caps, so total drug spending is not directly reduced.

For drugs used by low-income subsidy beneficiaries, the required manufacturer discount starts at just 2% of the negotiated price in 2024 and only reaches 10% in 2032, a slow phase-in that lightens the burden on manufacturers in early years.

Enrollees who fail to pay a monthly installment bill lose the smoothing option and go back to paying full cost-sharing at the pharmacy until they reach the annual threshold, with unsettled balances treated as plan losses.
The $3,100 annual cap still leaves enrollees with meaningful out-of-pocket exposure within the year, and the cap rises with inflation rather than being a fixed dollar amount.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The beneficiary relief is real: a hard annual cap, a smaller coverage gap, lower coinsurance, and monthly smoothing address the most common way seniors get hit with unaffordable drug bills. The honest costs are that the bill redistributes payment rather than lowering drug prices, it phases in the industry's contribution gently (especially for low-income-subsidy drugs), and it builds a complex third-party administration system for the discounts and monthly billing whose performance would depend on federal implementation.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Finance Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never took it up, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Cassidy introduced the Seniors Prescription Drug Relief Act on July 13, 2021, with Sen. Robert Menendez joining as the bill's one cosponsor.

The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on the day of introduction, and the action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — for the rest of the Congress.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill expired in committee without ever coming to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers and Part D insurers were spared the new point-of-sale discount duties and the sharply reduced federal reinsurance the bill would have imposed; seniors with high drug costs received no relief from this proposal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and Part D insurers

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator introduced the bill with one Democratic cosponsor; because it never reached a hearing or a vote, no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill imposes new point-of-sale discount obligations after the deductible, with civil penalties for noncompliance, but it also sunsets the existing coverage-gap discount program that required a 70% discount on brand drugs in the gap, and it starts the new discount at just 2% of the negotiated price for drugs used by low-income subsidy beneficiaries, reaching 10% only by 2032. The bill's death left manufacturers with neither obligation; many of the same benefit changes were later enacted through other legislation.

industries.industry: Part D insurers (prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage drug plans)
industries.note: Federal reinsurance payments to plans drop from 80% of catastrophic-phase costs to 20% for brand drugs (40% for other drugs) by 2026, and plans must administer automatic monthly-smoothing enrollment and absorb unsettled monthly balances as plan losses. The bill's failure left plans' existing reinsurance and benefit structure intact.

The bill protects pharmacy economics: it requires that the application of the monthly cost-smoothing option have no effect on amounts or timing of payments to pharmacies, and requires that pharmacies be reimbursed the discount difference within 14 days for electronic claims (30 days otherwise). It also requires pharmacies to notify enrollees when they may qualify for the smoothing option.
